paper_title: Wave Forcing: Towards Speed-of-Light Streaming Video Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Real-time long-video generation requires continuous output with consistent appearance and natural motion. Existing chunk-wise autoregressive methods face challenges in both generation efficiency and long-video quality: serialized denoising and history-cache refresh require two forward passes even with one-step denoising, and longer rollouts can degrade quality and cause camera drift. We propose Wave Forcing (WF), which co-designs generation, training, and execution for continuous video output with multi-step denoising. WF uses chunk-wise causal attention to access earlier, cleaner chunks before their denoising is complete, and distributes staggered denoising and cache-refresh stages across full-model replicas to achieve 1F1C: one output chunk per concurrent forward round after pipeline fill. To adapt the model to this continuous generation process, we develop a three-stage training procedure that successively introduces mixed-noise denoising, motion supervision, and causal adaptation using self-generated history. To execute this process efficiently, Wave Runtime (WaveRT) uses Wave Parallelism (WP) for early K/V delivery and communication-computation overlap, together with optimized kernels and pipelined VAE decoding. Experiments on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B show that 5-step WF maintains overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing while achieving higher Dynamic Degree on both short and long videos. Our system efficiency experiments show that 4-step WF achieves 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, yielding 7.07x the single-GPU end-to-end throughput. In DiT-only tests with matched SageAttention+W8A8 backends, denoising steps, and GPU counts, WP delivers up to 2.53x the throughput of the faster of the Ulysses and Ring context-parallel baselines across six model scales (1.3B-14B).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Real-time streaming video generation must sustain playable output with consistent appearance and natural motion. Chunk-wise autoregressive methods such as Self Forcing (SF) and Causal Forcing (CF) denoise each chunk conditioned on preceding content (Huang et al., 2025a; Zhu et al., 2026b). Under the clean-history caching convention adopted in this work, an additional forward pass, termed store, refreshes the key/value (K/V) history from the clean result. Sequential execution places denoising and store between consecutive outputs, yielding NF1C (N Forward Rounds, 1 Chunk Output). Thus, even one-step denoising requires two forward passes when store is included. We target 1F1C: one completed chunk per concurrent forward round after pipeline fill, while retaining every denoising update. Inspired by wavefront scheduling (Jin et al., 2016), earlier chunks execute later denoising stages while newer chunks execute earlier ones. These staggered tasks form moving wavefront (Fig. 1a). Assigning full-model replica to each denoising stage and the store stage creates bounded-width pipeline (Fig. 1c). To advance chunks before their predecessors finish, we use chunk-wise causal context: full attention within each chunk, cached history, and live context from earlier, cleaner chunks, with no dependence Equal contribution. (b) One later-layer K/V edge arrives before use. Other edges and initial waits are omitted. (c) Both schedules retain four denoising forwards plus store per chunk. Over five rounds, one SF replica emits one chunk, whereas five WF replicas emit five after fill. Wall-clock gains depend on stage costs and overlap. on later chunks. This directional conditioning accommodates differences in stage-wise progress and enables overlapped execution (Fig. 1b). Our staged training builds on mixed-noise joint denoising (Liu et al., 2026), uses teacher videos to supervise motion and framing, and adapts the model to causal inference with self-generated history. This generation structure and its training recipe together constitute Wave Forcing (WF). To turn this scheduling potential into shorter output intervals, Wave Runtime (WaveRT) implements Wave Parallelism (WP). Following GPU software-pipelining principles (NVIDIA, 2026a;b), WP exploits differences in stage-wise progress for early layer-wise K/V delivery and communication computation overlap, reducing exposed dependency waits. Data placement, kernel optimization, and load-balanced VAE pipeline parallelism complete the execution path from concurrent denoising to sustained video output. On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B (Wan et al., 2025), 5-step WF achieves overall quality comparable to 5-step Rolling Forcing (RF), with VBench Total scores of 81.64 versus 81.15 and VBench-Long Quality scores of 81.26 versus 81.18 (Huang et al., 2024; 2026b). Dynamic Degree increases from 51.39 to 94.44 on short videos and from 36.63 to 91.45 on 100-second videos. These gains are accompanied by better Subject Preservation (97.10 versus RFs 92.75) while maintaining low Camera Drift (0.37 versus RFs 0.17). In terms of system performance, 4-step WF with the BF16/FA3 backend achieves 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, yielding 7.07 end-to-end speedup over the 19.06-FPS single-GPU baseline  (Table 4)  . At this denoising speed, residual output-path overhead remains visible even with three-stage VAE pipelining, as discussed in Section 7. Across six model scales from 1.3B to 14B, WP outperforms the faster context-parallel (CP) baseline at five scales under BF16 and all six under Sage+W8A8, achieving 1.0252.530 its throughput under Sage+W8A8. System ablations and profiling further analyze how communication overlap, K/V placement, compute backends, and VAE stage balance affect runtime performance. Our contributions are threefold: Causal wavefront generation. We introduce Wave Forcing, allowing newer chunks to condition on earlier, cleaner chunks before their denoising completes. By pipelining denoising and cleanhistory cache refresh across full-model replicas, WF enables one completed chunk per concurrent forward round (1F1C) after pipeline fill while retaining all denoising updates. Training for continuous generation. We develop staged training recipe combining mixed-noise initialization, teacher-guided motion supervision, and causal adaptation with self-generated history. This adapts the model to wavefront inference, enabling strong motion and subject preservation over long rollouts at overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing. Efficient streaming execution. We build Wave Runtime to realize wavefront concurrency through early layer-wise K/V delivery, communicationcomputation overlap, and direct placement into attention buffers. With optimized local computation and load-balanced VAE decoding, the runtime translates stage concurrency into sustained end-to-end throughput, with efficiency validated across 1.3B14B models.

sections.title: 4 Wave Runtime
sections.content: WF exposes stage concurrency, but K/V dependencies can still stall attention. Wave Runtime (WaveRT) realizes Wave Parallelism (WP) by publishing K/V early from stage-owned replicas and overlapping delivery with computation when cleaner producers run ahead. We use SGLang Diffusions model implementation as the core execution backend (Zheng et al., 2024) of WaveRT.

For short videos, we report VBench (Huang et al., 2024) Total, Quality, Semantic, and Dynamic Degree, generating one 129-frame video per original prompt. For long videos, we report VBench-Long Quality and Dynamic Degree on 200 MovieGen (Polyak et al., 2024) prompts, generating 100-second videos. Long-video stability diagnostics. High motion scores can coexist with subject exit or unidirectional camera drift. sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: Efficient streaming video generation. Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2025a) reduces exposure bias by training autoregressive video diffusion on self-generated histories. SGF (Zhuang et al., 2026) restores gradient supervision for historical K/V through two-pass replay, while SGF+ (Su et al., 2026b) separates context-writing and denoising parameters to reduce gradient conflict. Other approaches include fewstep causal distillation (Yin et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026b) and mixed-noise denoising (Liu et al., 2026). AnyFlow (Gu et al., 2026) learns two-time flow maps with on-policy distillation for variable sampling budgets; Mask Forcing (Zhao et al., 2026b) perturbs DMD self-rollouts with dual-noise masking to improve teacher-mode coverage. For long-horizon streaming, Helios (Yuan et al., 2026) compresses historical and noisy context and simulates drifting during training. Vidu S1 (Zhang et al., 2026c) uses stage-aware noisy and clean history caches for real-time, voice-controlled character generation. Vidu S2 (Zhang et al., 2026b) introduces Self-Replay Forcing and supports dynamic references and streaming editing. These methods motivate studying training objectives together with the context available during streaming inference. Multi-chunk generation. Blockwise diffusion also appears in language modeling and action generation. D2F (Wang et al., 2025) conditions language generation on partially denoised predecessors, while MBD-LMs (Jin et al., 2026) align training with concurrent decoding of bounded set of blocks at heterogeneous noise levels. In vision-language-action models, BlockVLA (Wang et al., 2026c) adapts pretrained autoregressive models through block diffusion finetuning, and TBD-VLA (Lee et al., 2026) organizes actions into temporal blocks and supports asynchronous chunk execution through temporal inpainting. Multimodal Diffusion Forcing (Huang et al., 2025c) assigns noise levels across time and modalities to model dependencies within multimodal robot trajectories. These approaches illustrate different choices 9 of block dependencies; WF specifically trains video chunks to consume cleaner intermediate context through directed causal wavefront. Parallel execution. Ulysses (Jacobs et al., 2023) and Ring (Liu et al., 2024) partition individual forward passes, using all-to-all exchange and K/V circulation, respectively. Live Avatar and HiAR (Huang et al., 2025b; Zou et al., 2026) explore pipelined execution with fixed-timestep or matched-noise designs. WP instead schedules chunkstage tasks on full-model replicas (Sec. 5.5), adapting wavefront scheduling (Hou et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2016) alongside optimized attention and runtimes (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2024). Video evaluation. VBench (Huang et al., 2024) provides standardized quality, semantic, and motion measures. Our long-video comparisons (Sec. 5.1) show that high Quality and Dynamic Degree can coexist with subject loss and camera drift. We therefore supplement benchmark scores with targeted stability diagnostics; their scope and future alternatives are discussed in Secs. 7 and 8. These lines frame WFs joint design of causal conditioning, training, and execution, together with the evidence used to assess it. Section 7 examines the remaining methodological and system limits; Sec. 8 connects them to better evaluation, interactive generation, and world modeling.

sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.content: Our evaluation establishes streaming generation under fixed conditioning and the tested model, sampling, and hardware configurations. The following limits of the training and execution design discussed in Sec. 6 motivate the agenda in Sec. 8. Quality evaluation and diagnostic coverage. VBench-based scores do not fully characterize long-stream quality: in our comparisons, high Quality and Dynamic Degree coexist with subject disappearance and camera drift (Sec. 5.1). Subject Preservation and Camera Drift expose these failures, but rely on 100prompt subject-focused subset, tracking and identity association, and geometric heuristics (Appendix C.1). Their sensitivity to thresholds and missing observations, coverage of intentional scene changes, and agreement with human judgments remain to be established. They provide targeted diagnostics, with broader perceptual and semantic quality still requiring assessment. Output-path capacity and attribution. VAE pipelining overlaps and partitions decoding but does not remove its finite service capacity. The 1.3B BF16 configurations reach 147.58/134.81 DiT/E2E FPS at four steps and 104.82/96.46 at five steps (Tab. 1), with three and two VAE GPUs under the eight-GPU budget, respectively. These gaps are consistent with residual decoder/output-path limits. Aggregate timings, however, do not isolate VAE compute, transfers, queueing, or backpressure, and system DiT timing may reflect decoder interference. For 14B BF16, the gap narrows to 28.74 versus 28.64 DiT/E2E FPS (Tab. 4). Matched VAE-on/off runs and stage-level measurements are needed to identify bottlenecks and guide end-to-end resource allocation. Training complexity. WF currently uses complex multi-stage training procedure. An important direction is to simplify this procedure while preserving generation quality and long-video stability. Scalability at fixed sampling budget. For DiT denoising steps, WP uses denoising stages and one cache-refresh stage, each with full-model replica. Stage parallelism is therefore bounded at fixed step count, limiting the scale of single pipeline. Our experiments also show that WPs throughput advantage over CP narrows for larger models. These constraints motivate studying finer-grained or hybrid parallelism and resource sharing across streams. Interaction and serving scope. High steady-state throughput alone does not establish low input-tovisible-output latency. Online condition changes require deciding when inputs take effect in active chunks and how cached state is refreshed; the fixed-context equivalence argument in Appendix B.6 does not cover these updates. Prompt switching, camera/action control, closed-loop tasks, and multi-stream deadline guarantees require dedicated evaluation beyond the present fixed-conditioning experiments.

sections.title: 8 Future Work
sections.content: The limits in Sec. 7 define our research agenda: strengthen end-to-end streaming execution, enable online interaction, and then extend toward interactive world models. Serving research and richer quality evaluation support these capability extensions throughout. Appendix develops the task-specific questions. 10 End-to-end execution and scalability. We plan to profile decoder stages, transfers, queues, and backpressure to guide DiT/VAE resource allocation. To address WPs fixed-step scaling limit, we will study finer-grained execution and combinations with context parallelism, checking communication costs and causal dependencies under each design. Simplifying WFs training recipe while preserving motion and long-horizon stability remains parallel objective. Serving concurrent streams. StreamDiffusions image-stream batching (Kodaira et al., 2025) and StreamDiffusionV2s video-stream scheduling (Feng et al., 2026) motivate latency-aware batching. SlackServe (Xia et al., 2026) uses playout slack for resource and quality decisions, while PhysisServe (Physis AI Infra Team, 2026) explores fine-grained stage pipelining. Building on these directions, we aim to study admission control, batching, and resource allocation for concurrent WF streams while respecting their context dependencies. Evaluation should include startup delay, output jitter, playback stalls, fairness, and quality alongside throughput. Interactive streaming generation. The next capability is updating prompts during generation. LongLives KV recaching (Yang et al., 2026) provides starting point for coordinating new conditions with visual history. Extending WF requires defining which active chunks receive each update, refreshing affected state, and adapting training to condition changes. We will assess prompt-to-visible-output latency, prompt adherence, and visual continuity, rather than inferring responsiveness from output FPS. Interactive world models. Camera and action inputs further introduce feedback-dependent state evolution. We aim to explore both learned world prediction (Zhao et al., 2026a; Su et al., 2026a) and systems in which code or an engine maintains world state while video model renders observations (Chen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). The latter motivates adapting WF for structure-conditioned streaming rendering. Both routes require training under the corresponding control interface and evaluating control alignment, state consistency, and closed-loop behavior. They build on the execution and interaction work above and remain prospective extensions of WF. Richer quality evaluation. To address the metric limits above, we plan to incorporate streaminginteraction benchmarks such as StreamEval (StreamEval Team, 2026), which evaluates task execution and state consistency under timed inputs alongside visual quality. Long-video understanding methods such as StreamMeCo (Wang et al., 2026a) could help organize temporal evidence for an auxiliary quality judge. We aim to combine automatic diagnostics, understanding-based judgments, and human assessment, with explicit criteria for subject continuity, intended motion, and instruction execution. Such judges require timestamped evidence, calibration against human annotations, and checks for missed failures before their scores can support model comparisons.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: We present Wave Forcing, which jointly designs causal context, training strategies, and multi-GPU pipelining to denoise multiple video chunks concurrently. WF uses cleaner intermediate states of preceding chunks as context for subsequent chunks, with three-stage training adapting the model to mixed-noise contexts and self-generated histories. pipeline of full-model replicas then produces one video chunk per concurrent forward round after fill, while WaveRT overlaps K/V delivery with computation to reduce dependency waits. Experiments show that WF improves motion while maintaining overall generation quality and achieves high-throughput streaming video generation. These results demonstrate that jointly designing generation context, training, and execution can translate cross-chunk parallelism into practical gains in video generation efficiency.

sections.title: A Training Implementation Details
sections.content: Noise schedules and score networks. The 4-step schedule is [1000, 750, 500, 250] and the 5-step schedule is [1000, 800, 600, 400, 200], before timestep warping with shift factor 5. Both use three latent frames per chunk and preserve their respective schedules through all stages and inference. The frozen DMD teacher is bidirectional Wan2.1-T2V-14B. The trainable fake-score model starts from bidirectional Wan2.1-T2V1.3B and does not share weights with the causal student. It learns to denoise noisy, detached student predictions. Stage transitions transfer raw student weights and restart the fake-score model, optimizer, and EMA states. Evaluation uses the resulting EMA student. Off-policy targets and perceptual loss. Stage 2 uses 2048 training and 128 validation teacher examples generated by Wan2.1-T2V-14B with 50 denoising steps, guidance scale 3, and timestep shift 5. Each example contains 21 latent frames. The off-policy implementation samples consecutive chunks (3S latent frames), constructs student K/V from preceding clean teacher chunks, and re-noises the sampled chunks to form set of chunks at staggered noise levels. DMD and LPIPS are applied to the same clean prediction, with LPIPS weight 0.25 for both model versions. The fake-score update uses student predictions from these teacher-derived states. For LPIPS, latent spatial resolution is bilinearly reduced from 60 104 to 30 52, then decoded by frozen Wan VAE to 240 416 RGB frames. Every third decoded frame is evaluated. The 4-step training input contains 12 latent frames and decodes to 45 frames, giving 15 perceptual comparisons. The 5-step training input contains 15 latent frames and decodes to 57 frames, giving 19 comparisons. Decoded values are clamped to [1, 1], and VGG-based LPIPS is averaged over the sampled frames. Optimization and updates. The student and fake-score learning rates are 1.5 106 and 4 107, with Adam moments (0, 0.999). EMA uses decay 0.99 and starts after 200 training iterations. The training used eight workers with one sample each and no gradient accumulation, giving an effective batch size of eight. For the three-stage 4-step model, the 3000/1000/2000 training-loop iterations correspond to 600/1000/400 student updates and 3000/1000/2000 fake-score updates. The 5-step model starts from released RF weights and proceeds directly to Stage 2 (Sec. 3.2), so the Stage 1 iteration and update counts apply only to the 4-step model. Stage 1 and Stage 3 update the student once per five fake-score updates, whereas Stage 2 updates both models each iteration. Rollout visibility. The Stage 3 sampler selects RF, WF, or SF for the same student with equal probability. The WF path reuses the RF rollout implementation with chunk-wise causal attention to advance the wavefront: clean history and the same or earlier active chunks are visible, while later active chunks are masked. This matches Eq. (4). The RF and SF paths remain complementary training distributions.

sections.content: VBench protocol. We follow the standard VBench benchmark (Huang et al., 2024) with the original prompts, normalization, and weights, and scale scores to 0100. For detailed metric definitions, we refer readers to the VBench paper. All metrics are computed with the official standardized evaluation scripts. VBench-Long protocol. We report the VBench-Long Quality score and Dynamic Degree, scaled to 0100. Each method uses the same 200 MovieGen prompts and seed 42, generating 399 latent frames and 20 saving 1593 frames (about 100 seconds) at 16 FPS per video. Causal Forcing (Full Attn.) uses the EMA generator of the released chunkwise/longvideo.pt checkpoint with its native 4-step schedule and full attention, for both standard VBench and VBench-Long. Quality-generation setup. Rolling Forcing and Causal Forcing are evaluated in their own code repositories. RF with the causal mask and Wave Forcing use WaveRT with causal KV context, paged exchange, and time-partitioned VAE. The 4-step and 5-step models use 4+1+3 and 5+1+2 GPUs, respectively, ordered as denoising + Store + VAE. Checkpoint quality is evaluated with SDPA for standard inference and SageAttention for fast inference. Execution performance is measured separately using FA3 and dummy DiT weights. C.1 Long-video stability diagnostics Prompt subset. Both diagnostics require principal subject named in the prompt. fixed text rule first removes, for every method, group scenes, scenery, first-person views without stable visible subject, ambiguous principal entities, and prompts that ask the subject to disappear or transform. Of the 200 MovieGen prompts, 131 pass this rule. We then sample 100 of these prompts once at random and hold that subset fixed across methods, ablation studies, and both diagnostics. This subject-focused subset is distinct from the full 200-prompt VBench-Long evaluation. Subject Preservation. We measure the prompts principal-subject visibility. SAM3 tracks the text-specified entity at 8 FPS, giving 797 sampled frames per video. The initial binding is the largest detection in the first eight frames, and masked DINO (Caron et al., 2021) features decide which later detections share that identity. Let At be the current mask area and A0 the median mask area of the bound identity over the eight frames that begin at this binding. An associated box within 1% of the image border has visibility weight min(1, At/(0.18A0)), while any other associated detection has weight 1. new instance elsewhere keeps its own track while the recognized subject still has weight at least 0.5 and mask area at least 0.18A0. Frames without an associated detection have weight 0. The video score is 100 times the mean weight over all sampled frames, including frames before the binding and frames without support. Videos that never receive an initial binding, and videos whose binding was reviewed as incorrect, are left unscored. Camera Drift. Camera Drift measures persistent background motion with the subject moving toward an image boundary. We use the union of SAM3 detections for the text-specified entity at 8 FPS and point trajectories seeded outside those masks at 4 FPS. All distances are normalized by the image diagonal. For each image edge e, let ge and qe be the 5th and 90th percentiles of mask-pixel distances to that edge. Foreground outward velocity is the decrease in qe divided by the 0.25-second pair duration. Background velocity is the component-wise median of per-cell median track velocities over supported spatial cells, projected onto the same outward axis. We apply z(v) = sign(v) max(v 0.002, 0) to both velocities. Within the preceding five seconds, we use pairs with observed foreground and background motion. For either corrected velocity sequence, define outward displacement = max(0, 0.25 vt), path length = 0.25 vt, and response = (A/P)A2/(A2 + 0.12), with = 0 when = 0. These give foreground and background factors Fe and Be. Edge proximity is Ee = max(0, 1 ge/0.1). The instantaneous risk is maxe EeFeBe over edges with positive current foreground and background velocities, or zero if no edge qualifies. Thus, background motion with stationary subject does not incur drift penalty. To retain evidence after an exit, we require one second of consecutive outward foreground and background motion, at least two native pixels of foreground displacement, final ge within two native pixels of the boundary, and qe 0.1. After one second of consecutive explicitly empty masks, we hold the exits EeFe fixed and update Be from current background observations, without backfilling the confirmation interval. Missing background tracks can be replenished by points consistent with the existing motion layer, but new points contribute only after tracking through subsequent pair. This is geometric association, not an independent semantic background label. returning detection, uncertain mask, or scene cut ends the extension. Stopped or reversed background motion immediately gives zero risk and ends the extension after one consecutive observed second. Background gaps remain unscored, and later continuation is distinguished from uninterrupted support. The video score is 100 times the mean risk over valid 0.25-second intervals, so lower is better. Startup intervals before five seconds, unavailable current measurements, and windows crossing detected or unresolved cut remain unscored. Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2025a) completes all updates of one chunk before starting the next, reusing clean-history K/V. Its bounded history cache can evict the initial chunk, whereas RF retains it as an anchor. RF (Liu et al., 2026) advances consecutive mixed-noise chunks jointly, emitting one clean chunk per joint call after fill. Distributed RF retains every active chunks corresponding-layer K/V dependencies in both temporal directions. Communication overlap is still possible, but every consumer must respect those inputs. Both RF and WF are DAGs when unrolled over layers, so WF is distinguished by cleaner-only visibility, not merely by topological order. Stage-local and matched-noise pipelines. Live Avatar (Huang et al., 2025b) assigns fixed denoising timestep to each process. Earlier stages retain their original K/V snapshots as chunk progresses, and only latents move across stages. HiAR (Zou et al., 2026) instead builds causal hierarchy: each level uses freshly produced K/V from earlier chunks at its output timestep νs+1. The cache write for chunk can be fused with denoising chunk + 1. Its pipelined levels retain independent matched-noise caches and exchange latents, not layer-wise K/V between processes. This refreshed output-state context distinguishes HiAR from fixed-timestep snapshots. Wavefront execution. WF preserves current-layer live K/V from all legal cleaner chunks and store, and WP publishes this K/V across full-model replicas. Thus an anti-diagonal schedule alone does not imply WF conditioning. Its causal mask, cache rules, and training establish the model, while publication and readiness checks implement it. Appendix B.4 gives the cadence and resource accounting without equating steady output rate with first-output latency. sections.title: E Extended Future Work
sections.content: This appendix develops the interaction, serving, and world-model extensions in Sec. 8, following the training and execution limits in Sec. 7. These extensions have not been evaluated with WF. Online interaction and condition changes. LongLive (Yang et al., 2026) uses KV recaching to align visual context with an updated prompt; EditStream and LPM (Zhou et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026) explore interactive editing and character performance. WF extension must specify which prompt applies to each active chunk, which cached states need refreshing, and whether outstanding work is completed or discarded. The fixed-context equivalence argument in Appendix B.6 does not establish correctness across condition changes. Sustained FPS and interaction delay are distinct: evaluation should measure when an input first changes the displayed video, as well as adherence and continuity. Serving under streaming deadlines. StreamDiffusions image-stream batching (Kodaira et al., 2025) and StreamDiffusionV2s video-stream scheduling (Feng et al., 2026) motivate deadline-aware batching around WF. SlackServe (Xia et al., 2026) relates scheduling and quality choices to buffered playback time, while PhysisServes technical blog (Physis AI Infra Team, 2026) describes pipelining over transformer blocks and denoising steps, together with GPU time sharing. Future WF serving should study admission control, stream priorities, resource allocation, and finer-grained placement under its live-context dependencies. Changing sampling budgets also changes WPs available stage parallelism (Sec. 7); adopting another systems batching or state-reuse rules would therefore require checking WFs conditioning graph. Startup delay, output jitter, stall rate, and fairness should accompany throughput and quality measurements. Learning controlled world evolution. One route extends video prediction with structured controls. minWM and ForgeWM (Zhao et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026) study controllable few-step video generation; SolarWM (Huang et al., 2026a) emphasizes data standardization and causal adaptation; SANA-WM (Zhu et al., 2026a) explores hybrid linear attention for long-horizon generation; and OneWM (Su et al., 2026a) jointly learns world prediction and action generation. Integrating WF would require specifying when new camera or action inputs become available to in-flight chunks, validating state dependencies for each architecture, and assessing control fidelity, prediction consistency, and policy performance in closed-loop tasks. Executable world state and generative rendering. complementary route delegates persistent state, rules, and dynamics to code or an engine. Code World Model and Matrix-Game 4.0 (Chen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a) connect such state to video generation through visual proxies. StreamRender-H3 (Lu et al., 2026) and SolarRenderer (Fang et al., 2026) further motivate structure-conditioned streaming rendering. Here WF could supply an execution foundation for renderer trained to follow incoming structure, rather than taking responsibility for the engines dynamics. This would require aligned structure/video training and validation of temporal conditioning: StreamRender-H3 uses bidirectional attention within streaming window, whereas SolarRenderer includes block-causal variant. Neither establishes compatibility with WFs wavefront. Evaluation should check whether rendered observations preserve the underlying state and expose action effects quickly enough for feedback. Understanding-assisted quality evaluation. Following the metric limits in Sec. 7, future evaluator could combine local defect checks with long-horizon, instruction-aware judgments. StreamEval (StreamEval Team, 2026) evaluates timed requests and retained state alongside visual quality. StreamMeCo (Wang et al., 2026a) addresses efficient streaming video understanding, while MemForest (Wang et al., 2026b) provides event-centric memory compression and retrieval. These mechanisms could help video-understanding judge retrieve temporal evidence about entities, actions, and failures. Adapting them to quality judging requires human-calibrated validation: we should report supporting timestamps and unscorable intervals, assess agreement with human annotations, and test whether compressed memory loses brief defects or earlier facts. The goal is to complement our targeted diagnostics with broader, auditable quality assessment.
